chapters.title: Chapter 2: Framing Trading as a Machine Learning Problem

lessons.title: Feature Engineering for Price and Volume Data

children.text: MRF's shares have traded above ₹1 lakh each for years, the company has never split or bonused its stock. Feed a model MRF's raw closing price next to a penny stock trading at ₹8, and the model has no way of knowing these two numbers describe the same underlying idea, ownership of a company, at wildly different scales that have nothing to do with either company's quality. This lesson is about turning raw prices and volumes into features that actually generalize, across stocks and across time, instead of features that quietly memorize a single stock's price history.

body.text: A good feature describes something relative: how far a price has moved, how a stock's recent activity compares to its own history or its peers, not an absolute number like a raw price level or raw share volume. Absolute levels are not stationary and are not comparable across stocks, which makes them poor material for a model meant to learn general patterns.

children.text: Why Raw Price Levels Make Bad Features

A stock's raw price level drifts for reasons that have nothing to do with the pattern you are trying to capture: years of compounding, a bonus issue that halves the price overnight without changing anything about the business, or simply the fact that different companies choose different face values and share counts. A model trained on raw price levels from one multi-year window can fall apart the moment a stock undergoes a bonus issue or a stock split, or the moment you point it at a completely different stock with a different price scale. None of this is a modeling problem. It is a features problem, solved by describing price movement in relative terms instead of absolute ones.
Turning Prices Into Features: Returns, Not Levels

markDefs.definition: A return calculated as the natural logarithm of the ratio between two prices, rather than the simple percentage change. Log returns over consecutive periods add up cleanly, which makes them the more common choice in quant research.

children.text: The fix is to describe price action as returns rather than levels: how much did the price move, in percentage terms, not what was the price. A simple return over one day is today's close divided by yesterday's close, minus one. Quant research more often uses the

, the natural logarithm of that same ratio, because log returns over consecutive periods simply add together, while simple returns do not compound in a way that is convenient for statistics. From there, momentum features look backward over a window, how much has the stock returned over the past 20 days, and mean-reversion features measure distance from a recent average, how far today's close sits from its own 20-day moving average, as a percentage.

body.caption: Turning a raw price series into returns, momentum, and mean-reversion features
body.code:
import numpy as np

# Simple return over 1 day
df["ret_1d"] = df["close"].pct_change()

# Log return: additive across periods, the more common choice in quant research
df["log_ret_1d"] = np.log(df["close"] / df["close"].shift(1))

# Momentum feature: cumulative return over the past 20 days, as of yesterday's close
# (shifted by 1 so today's row never uses today's own close, avoiding the Lesson 3 leak)
df["mom_20d"] = df["close"].shift(1) / df["close"].shift(21) - 1

# Mean-reversion feature: how far today's close sits from its own 20-day average
df["dist_from_ma20"] = df["close"] / df["close"].rolling(20).mean() - 1

children.text: Volume Features: Context, Not Just the Raw Number

Raw traded volume has the same problem as raw price: a large-cap stock's typical daily volume and a small-cap stock's typical daily volume can differ by several orders of magnitude, and a single stock's own average volume tends to drift upward over the years simply as its free float grows. What matters for a feature is usually not how many shares traded, but whether today's activity was unusual relative to that stock's own recent normal, and how much rupee value actually changed hands, which is comparable across stocks with very different share prices in a way that raw share counts are not.

cells: Today's volume ÷ its own 20-day average volume
Removes the stock's own long-run volume trend and highlights unusual days
A comparable measure of money traded, not just share count, meaningful across stocks with very different prices
Distinguishes a big move on heavy volume, more conviction, from the same move on thin volume

children.text: Normalizing Across Stocks Without Leaking the Future

Two legitimate but different ways to make features comparable exist. Time-series normalization compares a stock to its own history, is today's move large relative to how this specific stock usually behaves. Cross-sectional normalization compares a stock to its peers on the same day, is this stock's momentum unusually strong relative to every other stock in the universe today. Both are useful, and answer genuinely different questions, but they get dangerous when a scaler meant to enforce either kind of normalization is fit incorrectly. Fitting a StandardScaler, or any normalization step, on your entire dataset before splitting into train and test is a data leak of exactly the kind Lesson 3 warned about: the scaler's mean and standard deviation end up quietly informed by test-period data that would not have existed yet at the time you are pretending to trade.

body.caption: Fitting a scaler correctly, without leaking the test period
body.code:
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler

# LEAKY: fitting on the full dataset lets test-period statistics influence the scaler
scaler = StandardScaler()
X_all_scaled = scaler.fit_transform(X_all)  # X_all includes rows from the test period

# SAFE: fit only on the training window, then apply those exact parameters to the test window
scaler = StandardScaler()
X_train_scaled = scaler.fit_transform(X_train)
X_test_scaled = scaler.transform(X_test)  # reuses X_train's mean and std, never re-fit on X_test

body.text: This exact scaler mistake is one of the most common, and most invisible, leaks in beginner ML-for-trading code from Lesson 3. It produces no error, the pipeline runs cleanly end to end, and the leak only shows up as a gap between backtest and live performance, usually a small one, but a real one, since the scaler learned a little more about the future than a live trader ever could.

columns.label: Time-Series Normalization
points: Compares a stock to its own historical behavior
Answers: is today unusual for this specific stock
Uses only that stock's own rolling mean and standard deviation
Useful for single-stock signals and regime detection

columns.label: Cross-Sectional Normalization
points: Compares a stock to all other stocks on the same day
Answers: is this stock unusual relative to its peers today
Uses the mean and standard deviation across the universe, on that date only
Useful for ranking and selecting stocks, such as picking the top decile by momentum

body.title: Spotting the leaky scaler
body.question: A researcher builds a feature set across 5 years of NSE data, fits a StandardScaler on the entire 5-year dataset, and then splits the scaled data chronologically into a training period and a later test period. What is the problem with this approach?
options: There is no problem, the split still happens in chronological order

The scaler's mean and standard deviation were computed using the full dataset, including the test period, so the test period has already quietly influenced the training data before the split ever happened
StandardScaler should never be used on financial data under any circumstances
The problem is that the data was not shuffled before scaling
body.explanation: A chronological split after fitting the scaler on everything does not undo the leak. The scaler's parameters, mean and standard deviation, already encode information from the test period. The scaler must be fit only on the training data, then applied unchanged to the test data, exactly as covered in Lesson 3.

body.title: Choosing the right normalization
body.scenario: A systematizing trader wants to build a model that selects the 20 NSE stocks, out of a universe of 200, with the strongest momentum each month, to hold for the following month.
body.prompt: Should this trader use time-series normalization, cross-sectional normalization, or both? Explain why.
body.modelAnswer: This is fundamentally a ranking and selection problem, choosing the strongest stocks relative to their peers on the same date, so cross-sectional normalization is the essential piece: momentum needs to be compared across all 200 stocks on the same day to decide who ranks in the top 20. Time-series normalization could still be layered in as an additional feature, for instance to flag whether a stock's current momentum is unusual relative to its own history, but on its own it would only describe a stock relative to itself, which cannot answer the actual question the trader is asking: who looks strongest today, compared to everyone else today.

cards.definition: A return calculated as the natural logarithm of the ratio between two prices, rather than the simple percentage change. Log returns over consecutive periods add up cleanly.
Today's traded volume divided by a stock's own recent average volume, used to flag unusually active or quiet trading days.
Comparing a value to a single stock's own historical mean and standard deviation, answering whether today is unusual for that specific stock.
Comparing a value across all stocks in a universe on the same date, answering whether a stock is unusual relative to its peers today.
A data leak that occurs when a normalization step, such as a StandardScaler, is fit on data that includes the test period, letting future statistics quietly influence training.

points: Raw price and volume levels are not stationary and are not comparable across stocks, which makes them poor features. Convert prices to returns and volume to relative measures instead.
Log returns are the more common choice in quant research because they add up cleanly across consecutive periods, unlike simple percentage returns.
Rupee turnover, price multiplied by volume, is a more comparable measure of trading activity across stocks than raw share volume.
Time-series normalization compares a stock to its own history; cross-sectional normalization compares a stock to its peers on the same day. Both are legitimate, but they answer different questions.

Fitting a scaler on the full dataset before splitting into train and test is a common, invisible data leak. Always fit normalization parameters on the training data only, then apply them unchanged to the test data.
